# Ether anaesthesia (`ether_anaesthesia`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: needs distillation, sulphuric_acid; helped by heat_sterilisation, antiseptics
- Core idea: Ether vapour can produce general anaesthesia, allowing surgery that would otherwise be unbearably painful. The depth of anaesthesia depends on the concentration inhaled and the patient’s breathing. Loss of consciousness can also mean loss of protective airway reflexes, airway obstruction or stopped breathing. Historical open-drop administration gave poor control of concentration. A trained attendant must manage the airway and ventilation throughout induction, surgery and recovery. Ether is highly flammable, and its dense vapour can travel along floors to a distant ignition source.
- Pitfalls:
  - Candles, lamps, fire or cautery in the room
  - Pouring on too much or leaving the cloth on when breathing weakens; nobody assigned to watch
  - A full stomach: the patient vomits and breathes it in
  - Crude ether still containing acid, or old ether kept in light and air, which forms explosive residues
  - Believing painless surgery is safe surgery; without clean hands and instruments more operations meant more deaths from infection
- History: china: c. AD 200 – Hua Tuo said to operate under a drug called mafeisan; recipe lost, account semi-legendary; east_asia: 1804 – Hanaoka Seishu (Japan) removes a breast tumour under a herbal general anaesthetic (tsusensan); europe: 1540 – Valerius Cordus describes making 'sweet oil of vitriol'; Paracelsus notes it puts chickens to sleep; 1800 Davy suggests nitrous oxide for surgery; 1847 Simpson introduces chloroform; americas: 1842 – Crawford Long (Georgia) operates under ether, unpublished until 1849; 1844 Wells tries nitrous oxide for dentistry; 16 October 1846 Morton's public demonstration in Boston
- Read:
  - Thomas Dormandy, The Worst of Evils: The Fight Against Pain (2006)
  - Stephanie J. Snow, Blessed Days of Anaesthesia: How Anaesthetics Changed the World (2008)
